title: Read what the package actually ships, and record two budgets nobody is watching

history.detail:
CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — round 1. Audited 7505224 with bookkeeping dcc3ffc, main checkout. Sprint file read fresh.

The sweep itself is complete and correct, and I verified that mechanically rather than reading the report. Three findings, all small, one of which will stop this release if nobody decides it first.

================================================================
REQ 1 — THE ENUMERATION IS COMPLETE. VERIFIED FILE FOR FILE.
================================================================

The criterion says a file present in the tarball and absent from the enumeration is the defect. I took `npm pack --dry-run --json`, extracted all 57 packed paths, and checked each against the sweep document: **0 files unaccounted for.** Every shipped file is named. That is the whole point of the sprint and it holds.

Both findings independently confirmed as real, in shipped files:
  run-role.js:55 and :444 carry a real downstream consumer's project identifier.
  launcher_test.js:154-155 carries the author's real home path, exposing OS username and layout.
And nothing was scrubbed in this commit — the diff adds a sweep document, a check, a .npmignore rule, an agent-file rule and a version bump. Req 2's instruction was followed.

The Windows-path line at launcher_test.js:192 is correctly reasoned rather than waved past: it uses the author's display name, and I confirmed that name is already public in package.json's own `author` field, so it discloses nothing package.json does not. Checking it and explaining why it is not a finding is better than not mentioning it.

REQ 5 — MET, and it names the pipeman base-profile probe explicitly, which is the criterion's own test. The generalisation is the useful part: "name, explicitly, in your own working notes, which exact object/file/list you are reading before you report what it shows." That is a checkable habit rather than "be careful", and it is the same shape as sprint 20's forced-denial fix.

REQ 6/7 — 0.1.23, one line. 177 OK, ALL LAUNCHER TESTS PASSED; ALL SMOKE TESTS PASSED.

REQ 3 — the check works, and I saw it work: verify-tarball.sh now reports
    LEAK: scripts/launcher_test.js contains this machine's home directory path (/Users/chrishobbs)
    TARBALL VERIFICATION FAILED
which is the real finding, caught by the real check, on a real pack. Verified in the direction that matters.

================================================================
FINDING 1 (blocking) — REQ 4's MEASUREMENT IS STALE, AND NAMES THE WRONG FILE
================================================================

The criterion is explicit: confirm the number matches a measurement taken at this commit, not a carried-forward figure, and re-measure it. I re-measured.

  recorded (run-role.js:1125-1126): master-controller.md, 14,083 chars, 43.0%, 18,684 remaining
  measured by me at this commit:    liveqa.md, 14,624 chars, 44.6%

Wrong file and wrong number. The cause is inside this commit: Req 5 added 1,586 characters to liveqa.md (body 12,496 -> 14,082), which pushed liveqa past master-controller. The measurement was taken before this sprint's own edit landed, so it is not carried forward from a previous sprint — it is stale against its own commit, which is the harder version of the defect to notice.

The practical risk is small (44.6% versus 43.0%, both comfortable) but the attribution matters for a budget item: anyone watching master-controller.md's growth as the constraint would be watching the wrong file, and this is a number recorded specifically so someone can watch it.

Worth naming the shape, since this sprint's own Req 5 is a rule about attributing to the right surface: the sprint that adds that rule records a budget attributed to the wrong file, because its own Req 5 edit changed which file was largest.

REQUIRED: re-measure at the final commit and correct both the file and the figure.

================================================================
FINDING 2 (blocking, and it is the one that will stall the release) — THE NEW CHECK BLOCKS PUBLISHING, AND NOBODY HAS DECIDED THAT
================================================================

verify-tarball.sh now fails on every run, by design, until the two findings are fixed — and Req 2 forbids fixing them in this sprint. That is correct and I am not disputing it.

But pipeman.md step 9.1 tells Pipeman to run verify-tarball.sh before publishing. Read it literally and the hard "stop, do not publish" is scoped to the sprint-data leak ("if it reports *either file* present in the tarball"), so this new failure is not textually covered. Read it as any sensible Pipeman would — a script that prints TARBALL VERIFICATION FAILED and exits non-zero — and publishing past it is not something a careful role does.

So this sprint cannot ship through its own documented release process without someone deciding, on the record, to publish past a failing pre-publish check. I grepped the sweep document and the sprint file: neither addresses it.

That is the transition-precondition pattern this framework has a rule about — Pipeman hits it, Pipeman cannot clear it, and there is no documented path through. It is exactly the kind of thing that stalls a release at the worst moment, with a role correctly refusing and no instruction telling it what to do instead.

REQUIRED, and the fix is a sentence, not code: name the consequence, in the sweep document and in the handoff, and say what Pipeman should do — publish past this specific known failure, or hold the release until the findings are fixed. **Which of those it is is the user's decision, not Dev Team's and not mine.** What must not happen is Pipeman discovering it unprompted.

================================================================
FINDING 3 (blocking, small) — THIS COMMIT ADDS A THIRD SHIPPED OCCURRENCE OF THE DISCLOSED NAME
================================================================

Finding 1 in the sweep records the consumer identifier at run-role.js:55 and :444. As of this commit it is also at scripts/verify-tarball.sh:106, inside the new check's own explanatory comment — and verify-tarball.sh is in the tarball (confirmed against the packed file list).

Verified it is new: `git show d958f31:scripts/verify-tarball.sh` contains zero occurrences; this commit introduces one.

Not a scrub violation and not a new disclosure of fact — the name is already public in run-role.js since 0.1.17. But the finding's recorded scope becomes inaccurate the moment 0.1.23 publishes, and the sweep's value is precisely that its scope statement is trustworthy. A disclosure record that undercounts its own footprint by one file, in the same commit that writes it, is the thing this sprint exists to prevent one level down.

REQUIRED: either reword the comment so it does not repeat the identifier (it can say "the consumer name in run-role.js" without naming it), or update Finding 1's location list to include it. The first is better — there is no reason for the new check's comment to add an occurrence.

================================================================
INFORMATIONAL
================================================================

1. My own audit notes reference the consumer name repeatedly, but they live in docs/sprints/state/*.json,
   which verify-tarball confirms is excluded from the package on every run. Checked rather than assumed,
   given the subject.
2. Carried, unchanged: every allowlist entry other than git and npm remains inferred; the empty-string
   ownedRepository declaration falling through silently. The --agents argv budget item is now
   measured and recorded by this sprint, so it comes off my carried list once Finding 1 is corrected.

RECOMMENDATION

Three fixes, one commit: re-measure Req 4 at the final commit, reword the new comment so it stops repeating the identifier, and name the release consequence with the decision left to the user. Then round 2 is short — the sweep itself needs no re-doing, and I will re-run the enumeration check and the measurement only.

One thing worth saying plainly, because it is the point of the sprint: this is the first time this project has read every file it ships. It found two real disclosures, one of them present in essentially every version ever published, and both are permanent. That result is worth more than a clean sweep would have been, and recording them unfixed — with a check that now fails loudly until someone decides — is the right disposition rather than a quiet scrub that would have left the published history exactly as exposed.
